p:ECU: Ecuador's money is the US dollar, adopted in January 2000 at 25,000 sucres to the dollar, so the Central Bank of Ecuador issues no currency of its own. It does not set policy either. The 1998 constitution had given the bank independence; the constitution that replaced it, sponsored by Rafael Correa's government and published on 20 October 2008, took it away. Article 303 makes the drafting of monetary, credit, foreign exchange and financial policy the exclusive power of the Executive, to be carried out through the Central Bank, and the bank's own website describes its job in those terms. The monetary board was replaced by a board of five members appointed by the president and confirmed by Congress. A monetary and fiscal history of Ecuador prepared for the University of Chicago lists 2008 as the suppression of central bank independence and says the constitution made the bank dependent on the executive branch, which became responsible for designing fiscal and monetary policy. Article 303 is still in force, so this is the standing arrangement rather than an episode with an end. Ecuador scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side being corruption in the country and the risk of money laundering in its banks. One case is recorded and it ended in conviction: on 8 January 2019 the National Court of Justice sentenced Pedro Delgado, a former president of the bank, to five years in prison, restitution of 788,855.94 dollars, forfeiture of assets and public apologies. Prosecutors described the crime as unlawful association while the court's own post called it illicit enrichment; the same source reports an earlier embezzlement conviction in 2015 carrying eight years, and says he allegedly allowed large loans without proper documents or guarantees while leading the bank, which is unproven. One career move is counted. Juan Diego Mosquera Pesantes was a delegate and member of the Monetary Board at the Banco Central del Ecuador in 1981, and has been a director and board member of Produbanco, formally Banco de la Produccion S.A., since 2014; the curriculum vitae Produbanco publishes for him also lists posts at Citibank Quito, where he was founding manager, Banco del Pichincha, Banco del Azuay, where he was a manager, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and BAC Corp Securities. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, pressing the bank to loosen policy, change the law and print money. The bank joined the World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which gives it advice, executive training and asset-management expertise rather than a mandate to run Ecuador's reserves. Its 2021 accounts were audited by Kreston Audit Services Ecuador. It holds 26.3 tonnes of gold, 27.7 percent of its reserves, and the country has had two systemic banking crises since 1970.
p:LBY: The Central Bank of Libya issues the dinar, and Britain's De La Rue prints the notes. Another run came from elsewhere: Goznak, the Russian state printer, printed dinars for the parallel eastern central bank in Benghazi, which is not internationally recognised, and Russian customs data cited by Reuters showed 4.5 billion dinars shipped between February and June 2019; Malta seized two containers on 1 November 2019, citing United Nations resolutions that recognise only the Tripoli government. The bank has signed a cooperation agreement under the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, aimed at better returns on its foreign currency reserves, which it describes as an exchange of expertise and capacity building rather than handing its reserves over to be managed. Four cases are recorded. The Misrata Criminal Court convicted two people of belonging to an organisation set up to seize 128 million US dollars and 5 million euros from the bank's Sirte branch in 2013 through coercion; one received 15 years in prison and a 2.5 million dinar fine, the other 13 years and a 50,000 dinar fine, and the Attorney General's Office reported the ruling in October 2023. In November 2022 the bank accused its deputy governor, Ali al-Hibri, of signing forged 50-dinar notes it said were printed in Russia and bore his signature, and Governor Saddek Elkaber asked the Attorney-General to pursue a complaint; that allegation is unproven. Two further matters come from Global Witness. Its investigation published on 19 February 2021 found that senior central bank officials hold paid directorships abroad and that Elkaber chairs a London bank indirectly owned by the central bank, which the report calls a conflict of interest; it cited nearly 2.5 billion dollars of private sector letters of credit approved between April and July 2020 and a 110 million dollar letter of credit for power equipment diverted to a company in the United Arab Emirates with a name almost identical to the original contractor's, and it states that it makes no allegation that any individual or bank broke the law. A companion report named that London bank as ABC International Bank, through which most Libyan letters of credit enter the international system, and said sources described mispricing, laundering and procurement fraud; no official finding of fraud followed. Both of those remain allegations. One long career runs through the bank: Saleh Ahmed Keshlaf began in its research department in 1985, was Director of the Governor's Office from 1999 to 2012, advised the research and statistics department from 2012 to 2024 and was reappointed Director of the Governor's Office in 2024. Alongside that he sat on the board of Arab Italian Bank (UBAE) from 2005 to 2012, on the Libyan Foreign Bank's supervisory committee from 2007 to 2012, as Deputy Chairman of the Libyan Financial Services Company from 2009 to 2024 and on Joumhourria Bank's supervisory committee from 2012 to 2022. The Libyan Foreign Bank and Joumhourria Bank are state institutions, so the move is filed as one inside the public sector and is not counted as a move into private finance. On 18 August 2024 the Tripoli-based Presidential Council decreed that Sadiq al-Kabir, governor since October 2011, be replaced by former deputy governor Mohamed Abdul Salam al-Shukri. The decree gave no official reason, and the east-based House of Representatives and the Supreme Council of State, both mandated to appoint governors under the constitutional document, called the firing illegitimate. A delegation from Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah's government then took over the governor's office, al-Kabir said he and other senior staff had fled the country because of militia threats, and banking operations were suspended. Deloitte audited the bank's accounts for 2021, and the United Nations Support Mission in Libya delivered the final reports of that audit through its Special Envoy, Kubis. Libya scores 50 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, more exposed than 96 percent of the 194 places with a figure, and 2.5 of 15 on how much it tells the public. It holds 146.7 tonnes of gold, 20.5 percent of its reserves.
p:SDN: The Central Bank of Sudan issues the Sudanese pound. It scores 45 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 85. On 9 February 2020 a body the transitional government had set up, the Empowerment Elimination, Anti-Corruption and Funds Recovery Committee, dissolved the bank's board of directors along with the boards of eleven other banks, and nine of the bank's managers were dismissed at the same time. The reason given was the bank's alleged links to the deposed government of Omar Al Bashir; that allegation is unproven, no individual board member was named and the evidence the committee relied on was not set out. In October 2025 Sovereignty Council head Abdel Fattah al-Burhan dismissed governor Burai Al-Siddiq Ali Ahmed after a dispute over the rules for buying and exporting gold, and appointed Amna Mirghani Hassan El Toum; deputy governor Mohamed Osman Ahmed Mohamed Khair was dismissed less than two weeks later. Three career moves are recorded. Ibrahim Mohammed Ali Nimir was general manager of the central bank from 1964 to 1967, then general manager of Elneilin Bank from 1970 to 1973, then returned as Governor and chairman of the board from 1973 to 1980; El Nilein's own group history says the bank, formed in 1963 out of a merger of Credit Lyonnais, the Arab Bank and the Red Sea Bank, was nationalised and became El Nilein Bank Group in 1970 and only became an independent entity in 2007, so that spell began in the year it passed into state hands. After his governorship he was general manager of National Bank from 1980 to 1982 and general manager of Workers National Bank from 1989 to 1992; Sudan nationalised its banks in 1970 and reversed course in stages afterwards, so those two legs are not settled either way. Mohamed Khair Ahmed Al-Zubair was Minister of Finance and National Economy from 2000 to 2001, held state minister and planning posts in the finance ministry through the 1980s and 1990s, was Vice President of the Bank of Sahel and Sahara Community, an intergovernmental bank, from 2002 to 2009, and became Governor of the Central Bank of Sudan in March 2011; the bank's own biography of him also lists former board seats, without dates, at the Saudi Sudanese Bank, where he was president of the board, the Financial Investment Bank and the Agricultural Bank of Sudan. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, both times pressing the bank to cut rates or ease and demanding that it print money. Its law scores 0.333 of 1 on one measure of independence, ranking 172 of 191, and it scores 1.5 of 15 on how much it tells the public. Its notes are made in the country: Dabanga reported in February 2019 that Sudan's new 200-pound banknote had gone into production at the Sudanese Company for Currency Printing, a domestic press the prime minister had visited that week. Who checks its books is the state rather than a firm: the bank's annual report presents its statement of financial position, profit and loss account, statement of changes in owner equity and cash flow statement for the year ended 31 December 2015 as audited by the National Audit Chamber, the body behind the Central Bank of Sudan Act 2002, which requires the accounts to be audited in accordance with the General Audit Chambers Act 1999 without naming an auditor. No documented case at the central bank was found, which is not proof none happened; Reporters Without Borders rates the situation for journalists here as very serious in its 2026 index, so the court reports a case would be found in may not exist or may not be publishable.
p:SRB: The National Bank of Serbia issues the Serbian dinar, and makes its own notes and coins at its Institute for Manufacturing Banknotes and Coins at Topčider, which was built from 1927, began operating in December 1929 as the institute of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, gained a mint in 1937 and also produces for foreign countries. A bill, expected to pass on 15 July, would have placed the bank under government control and allowed the dismissal of governor Mladjan Dinkic: Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic wanted a devaluation Dinkic resisted, and members of the DOS coalition said a party official cannot be governor. Dinkic said the law would make the bank dependent on government and parliament; the authorities said his claims had no foundation. On 18 July 2003 he resigned, with two of the bank's three deputy governors, after parliament passed a law letting members of parliament nominate and appoint the bank's top officials; Energy Minister Kori Udovicki was nominated to succeed him. On 11 January 2006 police arrested vice-governor Dejan Simić, along with Vladimir Zagrađanin, on suspicion of taking bribes; an investigation was ordered and the bank's Council removed him on 16 January 2006, but no indictment, verdict or acquittal followed, so the suspicion is unproven. On 10 May 2011 Erste Bank Hungary named a former governor, Radovan Jelašić, its chairman and chief executive, to start on 1 June 2011 subject to approval by the Hungarian market regulators. Serbia keeps its gold at home rather than with a custodian abroad. It holds 54.6 tonnes in all, 20.9 percent of its reserves. The bank's annual report for 2024 sets out the make-up of the foreign exchange reserves at 31 December 2024 as foreign securities at 59.16 percent, money in accounts abroad at 22.04 percent, gold in the bank's own vaults at 13.26 percent, and foreign cash and special drawing rights; the whole holding sits in those vaults in Belgrade, with no foreign custodian, which is storage rather than management. Ernst & Young d.o.o. Beograd audited the accounts for 2025. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks themselves, and has two currency swap lines with China, one re-signed on 28 May 2026 for 5 billion yuan against 74 billion dinars and running five years from the re-signing, and an earlier agreement of June 2016 for 1.5 billion yuan. Serbia scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, less exposed than 76 percent of the 194 places with a figure.
p:IRL: Ireland uses the euro, so its interest rates are set not by the Central Bank of Ireland but by the European Central Bank, for the 21 European Union states that use the currency; Bulgaria joined on 1 January 2026, at 1.95583 lev per euro, and its governor took a seat on the ECB's Governing Council. The Irish bank's books are checked from outside by Grant Thornton Ireland, under a term covering 2023 to 2027, with the Comptroller and Auditor General also auditing the accounts. Its gold bars are held at the Bank of England, which stores them rather than manages them, and the remaining coin stocks stay at the Central Bank of Ireland. The bank also pays outside firms to run its own portfolio of shares, and the contracts are public. A tender with reference 2016P038, for equity management services, went to Amundi Asset Management of 90 Boulevard Pasteur in Paris, for a contract valued at 700,000 euro excluding value added tax. The next round, reference 2022P012, appointed UBS Asset Management (UK) Ltd of 5 Broadgate, London, for a contract valued at 10 million euro excluding value added tax. In 2008 and 2009 the financial regulator, Neary, said he would retire early over the regulator's handling of 87 million euros in secret directors' loans at Anglo Irish Bank; an internal committee found the matter, discovered in January 2008, was not pursued, partly because a letter from Anglo went missing, and Neary said he was not told until the finance minister raised it in December 2008. Two further findings sit at the European Central Bank. In case 1697/2016/ANA the European Ombudsman found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that president Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a club whose members include central bankers and private bankers, saying it was not in keeping with the ECB's independence; the bank declined and he kept it. And a speech of 18 May 2015, in which Coeure told a private evening event in London that the bank would front-load asset purchases, was published only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error; Draghi said no market-sensitive information was revealed. Seven career moves run between these banks and private finance, among them Matthew Elderfield, the Irish deputy governor and financial regulator, hired by Lloyds Banking Group as director for conduct and compliance from October 2013, and Otmar Issing, a former ECB chief economist who became an international adviser to Goldman Sachs in 2006. The sharpest pressure on Ireland's central bank came from outside the country. Emergency lending to banks is paid out by the Central Bank of Ireland but has to be allowed by the European Central Bank's governing council, and on 19 November 2010 the ECB's president, Jean-Claude Trichet, wrote to the finance minister, Brian Lenihan, in a letter marked secret, saying that further emergency lending would be authorised only if Ireland committed in writing to apply for an international rescue programme, along with commitments on austerity, bank recapitalisation and repayment of the liquidity. Support to Irish banks had passed 50 billion euros by then. Lenihan, who had insisted publicly the week before that Ireland needed no bailout, wrote back accepting that Sunday, and Ireland applied on 21 November. The ECB refused to publish the letter for four years and released it on 6 November 2014, after the European Ombudsman and an Irish member of the European Parliament pressed for it and after The Irish Times had obtained and printed it; the ECB's statement with the release said documentation showed domestic factors pushed Ireland towards the programme. Ireland scores 23 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, less exposed than 91 percent of the 194 places with a figure.
p:COL: The Bank of the Republic issues Colombia's peso and prints it itself, at its own banknote works, with a coin plant at Ibagué in Tolima; it is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks themselves. One case is recorded and it ended in the officials' favour: two of them were investigated in 2011 for allegedly giving reserved information about people and companies to officials of the DAS security agency and received a one-month suspension, but in January 2011 the bank reported that the Procuraduría's second-instance ruling revoked the suspension, recognising that they had broken no rule. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, each time to cut rates. On 31 July 2025, after the board voted 4 to 3 to hold the rate at 9.25 percent, President Gustavo Petro accused the bank of wanting to finish off the economy and of having an electoral bet. Much of the work of investing Colombia's international reserves, the foreign money the central bank keeps in hand, is given to outside firms. The bank's reserves management report counts seven of them each running a dedicated, actively managed portfolio of those reserves at 31 December 2024, among them JPMorgan Asset Management (UK) Limited, Wellington Management Company LLP, Goldman Sachs Asset Management L.P., State Street Global Advisors Trust Co., UBS Asset Management (Americas) Inc. and Pacific Investment Management Company LLC, known as Pimco. Beyond those private managers, on the same date the bank held 914.79 million US dollars in the Bank for International Settlements' Chinese government and central bank bond pools and 287.59 million in its global corporate debt pool, funds open only to central banks. Amundi won a mandate in 2023, as one of eight outside managers, running an active fixed income programme covering Treasuries, mortgage-backed securities and G10 currencies for 1.7 billion US dollars of assets; the central bank was impressed by Amundi's knowledge-transfer proposal when screening managers. The reserve gold, 4.7 tonnes or 1 percent of reserves, is in the custody of the Bank of England, which stores it rather than manages it. Two career moves are recorded. Leonardo Villar became general manager in January 2021, after serving as an Executive Director at the International Monetary Fund from November 2018 to October 2020 and alternate Executive Director in November and December 2020. Gerardo Hernández Correa spent sixteen years at the Bank of the Republic as a board member, executive manager and secretary of the board, was Colombia's financial superintendent for six years, became vice-president for legal affairs at Banco de Bogotá in 2021, and on 27 June 2024 was named president of Banco AV Villas, replacing Juan Camilo Ángel; both are commercial banks, and the same report states that Grupo Aval, a private financial conglomerate rather than a state body, holds controlling stakes in financial entities including Banco AV Villas. The accounts for the year ended 31 December 2024 were checked by the Auditor General del Banco de la República, an office inside the bank, in a report dated 27 January 2025. Colombia scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, less exposed than 80 percent of the 194 places with a figure, and 8 of 15 on how much it tells the public. There have been two systemic banking crises since 1970.
p:TLS: Timor-Leste has its own central bank, the Banco Central de Timor-Leste, created in 2001, but not its own currency: it uses the US dollar. The International Monetary Fund's 2023 classification lists it among the places with no separate legal tender and the dollar as anchor. The bank is also the day-to-day manager of the country's Petroleum Fund, and it hires outside firms to run parts of that money. Its quarterly report for 30 June 2025 sets out six managers and their mandates: the Bank for International Settlements on a hedged global developed-market sovereign bond mandate, State Street Global Advisors on an equity factor mandate and an international equity passive mandate, Schroders on an equity factor mandate, BlackRock on an international equity passive mandate, and Barings LLC and Franklin Templeton each on a 1-10 years US TIPS mandate. The report says the outside managers' investments stayed within their mandates during the quarter. One case is recorded. In its report and opinion on the 2019 General State Account, the country's Court of Accounts found that 6.6 million US dollars of European Union direct budget support, held in three bank accounts at the central bank, was not booked as state revenue, so 2019 state revenue was understated by that amount, and that the 2.3 million US dollars spent from those accounts was spent outside the state budget and the General State Account. The same report recorded a closing accounting balance of 4.4 million US dollars against a cash balance at the central bank of 5.2 million. One career move is recorded, every employer in it a public or multilateral body: Helder Lopes, governor from 2023 to 2029, had been Minister of Finance and Vice Minister of Finance, an adviser to the President and to the Ministry of Finance, and earlier a senior economist on the Asian Development Bank's private sector development initiative in Timor-Leste. Timor-Leste scores 34 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 64 percent of the 194 places with a figure. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, 57, with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 44 of 100 for 2025. The independence the law gives the bank is comparatively strong, 0.777 of 1 and rank 50 of 191. Ernst & Young Audit & Associados - SROC, S.A. audited the 2023 accounts.
